articles.title: Postgres Training Backups: Node.js pg_dump Gzip Streams for 2026 Object Retention
articles.excerpt: The reliable default for an edtech backup is a streamed pg_dump compressed with gzip, uploaded as a private object, and retained by a policy that can be replayed from metadata. Large-file throughput i…
articles.body: The reliable default for an edtech backup is a streamed pg_dump compressed with gzip, uploaded as a private object, and retained by a policy that can be replayed from metadata. Large-file throughput is the deciding constraint: keep the web process out of the byte path, make each archive addressable, and test restore rather than treating an upload receipt as proof. Short answer: run the dump in a worker, stream compression into multipart object storage, write an immutable manifest beside it, and issue a signed restore URL only after a successful integrity check. A retention rule should be data, not a cron comment.

articles.title: A download archive needs a restart policy
articles.excerpt: A folder can exist and still be an unfinished download, so I want an archive job to tell me what happened when it finds that folder again. My own job had a gap there. It skipped the existing folder wi…
articles.body: A folder can exist and still be an unfinished download, so I want an archive job to tell me what happened when it finds that folder again. My own job had a gap there. It skipped the existing folder without checking its contents, recorded the status as existing , and returned a failed batch at the end. That kept it from claiming success, but it also meant a rerun couldn't certify a completed download. I found that by reading the script after a successful model archive, where all seven repositories were marked verified and the recorded checksum checks passed for each one. The original run hadn't shown me an interruption. I tested the restart branch separately with a fake existing directory and mocked download commands.

articles.title: The Shift Handoff: Turning Chat Queues into Executable Summaries
articles.excerpt: The worst five minutes of any support shift are the first ones. The night team goes home, the day team opens the queue, and the only bridge between them is a paragraph of prose in a group chat — if th…
articles.body: The worst five minutes of any support shift are the first ones. The night team goes home, the day team opens the queue, and the only bridge between them is a paragraph of prose in a group chat — if the night team remembered to write it. Everything that actually matters is scattered across threads: a promise made to a customer at 2am, a buyer typing in short angry bursts, a promo rule that changed at midnight. Prose is a lossy serialization format for all of that. The fix is not nicer prose. It is treating the shift handoff as an executable summary: structured data with owners, states, and next actions — written so a person can act on it in minutes, and so a machine can read it at all. Why Prose Handoffs Fail Free-text handoffs fail in predictable ways.

articles.title: How to Compress an Image to a Specific KB Size Without Obvious Quality Loss
articles.excerpt: A website, application, or email form may reject a photo that is larger than its file-size limit. If the limit is 100 KB, the practical goal is to create a clear image that comes in at or below 100 KB…
articles.body: A website, application, or email form may reject a photo that is larger than its file-size limit. If the limit is 100 KB, the practical goal is to create a clear image that comes in at or below 100 KB—and then check that the destination accepts it. A target-size setting is a useful starting point, but image compression has trade-offs. A detailed photograph can need more data than a simple graphic, and the same settings may produce different file sizes for different images. The reliable workflow is to set a maximum, inspect the result, and adjust dimensions or format if needed. What does “compress to 100 KB” mean? In most upload tasks, “compress to 100 KB” means make the file no larger than 100 KB. It does not mean the file must be exactly 100 KB.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.body: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

articles.body: There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with. But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer? more…

articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
articles.excerpt: Just a day after SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket back at the launch pad for the first time ever, Elon Musk told us that the spacecraft will get even bigger.
articles.body: As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15).

articles.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 is approaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.
articles.body: After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.
